item.title: NYPD warns public to avoid Times Square amid reports of officer-involved shooting
item.description: The NYPD urged the public to avoid West 43rd Street and Seventh Avenue in Times Square as officers investigated the reported shooting incident.
item.content:encoded:
The NYPD urged people to avoid a busy Times Square intersection Monday afternoon as officers investigated an incident amid reports of an officer-involved shooting.

Police warned the public to avoid West 43rd Street and Seventh Avenue and expect delays in the surrounding area.

A witness claimed on social media that a woman was "running around stabbing people." A video posted to social media showed a woman wielding what appeared to be a knife. She appears to approach a group of police officers with the knife and is shot.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Bryan Kohberger's new lawyer says key questions may soon get answers in court
item.description: Bryan Kohberger's new lawyer says upcoming filings will address unanswered questions about the Idaho student murders guilty plea withdrawal.
item.content:encoded:
Bryan Kohberger's newest lawyer says upcoming filings and a potential evidentiary hearing will shed new light on the Idaho student murders case while their immediate legal fight concerns the constitutionality of the plea his client is attempting to withdraw.

"We think the [amended] PCR and evidentiary hearing will naturally address some of the outstanding and unanswered questions," Jason Goldman, a New York-based attorney who is joining Kohberger's team, told Fox News Digital Monday. "That said, the main priority right now is to scrutinize the constitutional issues surrounding Bryan's plea."

Kohberger, in a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief filed in July, told the court he had ineffective counsel, that his guilty plea was "not knowingly or voluntarily entered because it was induced by unkept promises" and that it was "not voluntarily entered because of threats asserted by petitioner's (Kohberger's) legal counsel."

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES

"The circumstances surrounding Bryan's plea — and what occurred in the critical days leading up to it — deserve careful, independent judicial scrutiny," Goldman said. "Some of those circumstances are already part of the public record. Others are not."

He also said that the support Kohberger receives from his family is part of why he agreed to join the case.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S MOTHER CALLED HIM 'MY ANGEL' AND INSISTED POLICE MADE A 'REALLY, REALLY BAD MISTAKE': BOOK

"Most family and friends run for the hills when a loved one is quietly arrested, let alone charged with a highly-publicized murder," he said. "The unwavering support Bryan maintains speaks volumes." 

Judge Steven Hippler set a Nov. 13 deadline for Kohberger's lawyers to file an amended petition which is expected to be written by attorneys and include more in-depth legal arguments than the handwritten petition Kohberger submitted in July.

BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL

Idaho defense attorney Greg Rauch was appointed to represent Kohberger last month. Goldman said he would be joining as out-of-state counsel but is not yet officially on the docket.

Prosecutors have asked the judge to dismiss Kohberger's petition on numerous grounds, but Kohberger's lawyers filed a motion last week to have the judge removed from the case and to change the venue back to Moscow, Idaho, where the offices of Rauch and the Latah County Prosecuting Attorney are both located.

Kohberger had previously sought a change of venue out of Latah County, where the murders took place, which landed him in front of Hippler in Ada County.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"The motion speaks for itself," Goldman said. "We must ensure that the serious constitutional questions at play are heard in a forum whose impartiality and neutrality cannot be questioned."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The motion, signed by Rauch, questions Hippler's impartiality, noting that he declined to give Kohberger's former defense team more time when they said they were not finished with discovery review weeks before trial.

READ THE MOTION:

Rauch also took issue with some of the language Hippler has since used to describe his client: "someone in whom the Court could identify nothing remaining that was 'good or intrinsically human.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Kohberger, 31, last year pleaded guilty to four counts of first-degree murder and a felony burglary charge for the 2022 stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20.

He did not give a motive.

GOT A TIP?

In a motion filed last week, Deputy Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl asked for a transcript of Kohberger's July 2, 2025, change of plea hearing, in which Kohberger's own words could be used to rebut the new claims in his petition.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Hippler set a Nov. 13 deadline — four years to the day after the murders — for Kohberger's legal team to file an amended petition and set aside two potential dates for a status conference and evidentiary hearing next year.

KOHBERGER DEFENSE EXPERT WANTS HIS LAWYERS UNDER OATH AFTER KILLER CITES FINDINGS IN BID TO UNDO GUILTY PLEA

Hearings on the recusal and venue motions could be held before then.

"We will let the evidence and the filings speak in due course," Goldman told Fox News Digital. "Stay tuned."

item.title: Matthew Berry details how he reported Tom Brady signing with Tampa Bay while drunk at a bar with team official
item.description: Matthew Berry revealed to OutKick how a late-night bar encounter at the NFL Combine led him to first report Tom Brady's move to Tampa Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Do you remember who first reported that Tom Brady would join the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2020?

Matthew Berry thought about the question for a brief moment before remembering. "Oh, I believe it was me," he told OutKick.

For context, Brady announced his departure from the New England Patriots weeks before signing with Tampa Bay. At the time, his rumored destinations included the Los Angeles Chargers, Las Vegas Raiders and Indianapolis Colts. No one had mentioned the Buccaneers.

MATTHEW BERRY DISCUSSES WHETHER HE'D HIRE DIANNA RUSSINI FOR HIS BUDDING FANTASY FOOTBALL EMPIRE

Then, after the NFL Combine, Berry wrote in his annual rumors column that he would bet on Brady heading to Tampa. He told OutKick he was quite confident about his prediction at the time.

"I won’t give away my source, but I will tell you how I came across the information. I was at the NFL Combine, and it was about 2 a.m., and I was in a bar. I met somebody who worked for the Buccaneers organization," he explained.

"We were drinking for an hour and were hammered. This particular person tells me, ‘I think we have a shot at Brady.’ And I’m like, ‘No, you don’t.’"

Berry added: "And this person tells me, ‘No, man. We worked him out. We’ve had conversations with him. We think it’s down to us and, I think he said, the Raiders. He goes, Gisele wants a South Florida team to make it easier for her to get home, to fly out of a Florida airport."

As they continued drinking, Berry realized the person was, in fact, serious.

"The more he talked, the more convinced this person sounded. I thought, ‘Well, okay.’ These are things that I hear drunk in a bar."

MATTHEW BERRY HAS HAD TALKS WITH ESPN ABOUT A RETURN, FOLLOWING PAT MCAFEE MODEL

As I mentioned to Berry during the conversation, I remember reading his report and asking an NFL insider about it. The insider said they had not heard that. Fans and media were also skeptical that a fantasy football guru, rather than a traditional insider, would have the correct information about one of the biggest transactions in NFL history.

Later that night, the insider texted me back: "Berry is onto something."

Brady eventually signed with Tampa Bay and led the Buccaneers to a Super Bowl victory in his first season there.

The takeaway is obvious. For those who want to break major NFL stories, the real information is not obtained at journalism school, but while drunk in a bar at 2 a.m.

Berry appreciated that we asked him about the scoop. "No one has ever brought that up before. Thank you."

You can watch OutKick's full interview with Matthew Berry on YouTube here.

item.title: Mom loses grip on daughter as passenger ferry capsizes with 20 people still missing
item.description: A mother describes losing her grip on her 12-year-old daughter as the Cyprus ferry capsized, with some 20 passengers still missing in waters over 1,600 feet deep.
item.content:encoded:
A ferry carrying 267 passengers and crew capsized off the northern coast of Cyprus, leaving at least eight people dead and 20 others missing as search efforts continued Monday.

The vessel was traveling from Kyrenia in northern Cyprus to the Turkish port of Tasucu when it began taking on water shortly after leaving port Sunday, according to Reuters.

Survivors were rescued from the water and from the overturned ferry as nearby vessels and coast guard crews responded, Reuters reported.

CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING

Among those still missing Monday were siblings Miray Bicer, 12, and Mehmet Asaf Bicer, 6, who had been visiting Cyprus with their family, the outlet reported. 

Their mother, Ayten Bicer, described the struggle to hold onto her daughter as the vessel overturned.

"She was saying, 'Don't let go,'" Bicer told Reuters. "And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go."

A suitcase fell on Bicer during the chaos, causing her to lose her grip on the girl. 

She managed to grab her daughter's foot, but said oil from the vessel made the area slippery and the child slipped away.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Officials raised the number of people considered missing from 18 to 20 on Monday after checking passenger records against the list of survivors, according to Reuters.

The search has also been complicated by the location of the wreckage, which lies in water more than 1,600 feet deep.

Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman said a ship from Turkey equipped to assist with work on the seabed was expected to arrive on Tuesday, Reuters reported. 

It remained unclear whether anyone was trapped inside the sunken ferry.

Authorities have also begun investigating what may have caused the vessel to sink.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Nine people connected to the ferry's operations were detained as part of the investigation, according to Reuters. Authorities said the vessel had a valid seaworthiness certificate.

Questions also remain about the conditions at the time of the disaster.

Northern Cyprus Prime Minister Unal Ustel said the ferry encountered adverse weather and began taking on water about 15 minutes after departure, according to the Associated Press (AP). 

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Erhurman, however, said weather conditions "were not bad" and cautioned against speculating about the cause of the sinking, the outlet reported.

The internationally recognized government of Cyprus also offered to provide assistance with the search-and-rescue operation, according to AP.

Reuters and The Associated Press contributed reporting.

item.title: Kansas City Chiefs may have ruined Jack Pyburn's plan to make big money at LSU by giving him a job in the NFL
item.description: Jack Pyburn was set to earn more at LSU than his NFL rookie salary, but the Kansas City Chiefs claimed the linebacker off waivers from Tampa Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Folks who track such things last week were estimating that Jack Pyburn could make around $1 million in 2026 if he was cut by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and allowed to return to college at LSU. Except, well, the Kansas City Chiefs had other plans.

The Chiefs on Monday afternoon claimed the linebacker off waivers from the Bucs, per the NFL waiver wire.

That means Pyburn's NFL career continues as a member of the Chiefs' 53-man roster.

NCAA CREATED THIS MESS, NOW LSU SET TO MAKE DAE’QUAN WRIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S FIRST NFL RETURNEE

It also means Pyburn is seemingly headed for a pay cut by being in the NFL rather than back in college.

Yes, crazy world.

Pyburn's rookie salary is scheduled to be $885,000. And that is less than the $1 million he was expected to make in college.

So we have reached the critical juncture where the NIL rules and countless court filings and rulings on eligibility have turned college football into something of a financial competitor for the NFL in the case of some players.

MATT RHULE SOUNDS ALARM ON NFL RETURNEES, $45 MILLION ROSTERS AND COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S PAYROLL PROBLEM

It's been that way before.

There have been examples where quarterbacks forego their final years in college and the sizeable pay they might have earned in that season, and go to the NFL to take a financial shave.

But that's quarterbacks.

Stars.

And it is their choice to start what promises to be a lucrative career longterm.

Jack Pyburn?

He was not drafted in April coming out of LSU. He played only one season there after playing at the University of Florida in 2023 and 2024.

Pyburn played in 12 games with 11 starts at LSU and collected 52 tackles with 2 sacks and 5.5 tackles for loss. That's nice.

But that doesn't scream $1 million nice.

NCAA WINS TENTH CIRCUIT 'STAY', BUT FACES MORE ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FROM 2022 CLASS ATHLETES IN CHAOTIC TIME

And how did we get here?

Pyburn was part of a lawsuit filed by more than 30 athletes in Louisiana that won a temporary restraining order allowing them to play in college in the 2026 academic year.

Pyburn and other players meeting certain criteria who signed with or were drafted by NFL teams were allowed to return to school as long as they could terminate their pro contracts and repay any pro earnings.

Pyburn was reportedly ready to do that with the Bucs because they were expected to cut him – as they eventually did. They had guaranteed him $115,000, including a $15,000 signing bonus.

But now that contract is not terminated. It and the rights to Pyburn belong to the Chiefs.

Pyburn, by the way, reportedly informed LSU that he is withdrawing his name from the ongoing eligibility lawsuit and will remain in the NFL – not that the Chiefs gave him a choice, really.

item.title: Tips for your fantasy football draft: How to build a winning team without overthinking it
item.description: Fantasy football draft strategy goes beyond player rankings. League scoring rules, PPR settings, roster construction, and ADP all shape your picks.
item.content:encoded:
It's that time of year again. You've read the rankings, listened to the podcasts, watched some preseason football and probably done at least one mock draft that completely fell apart by the fifth round (or you literally stopped paying attention after round three).

You've got a strategy, and you're ready for your actual fantasy football draft.

So, naturally, the guy in your league who hasn't done a second of research and shows up 10 minutes late asking, "Wait, Mike Evans is on the 49ers now?" is probably going to win the championship.

That's fantasy football.

There are hundreds, probably thousands, of fantasy football analysts on the internet, and many of them are very good at what they do. They'll tell you which running backs are undervalued, which rookie wide receivers are about to break out and which quarterback is being drafted three rounds too early.

TIME TO FACE FACTS: FANTASY FOOTBALL PUNISHMENTS HAVE OFFICIALLY JUMPED THE SHARK IN 2026

Find an analyst whose opinion you trust. Better yet, find a few.

That's not what we're doing here.

Instead, I want to talk about general fantasy football draft strategy. I've been playing fantasy football for a long time, in a lot of different leagues with a lot of different people, and there are certain mistakes that people make over and over again.

Avoiding a few of them won't guarantee you a championship. Nothing will.

But it certainly won't hurt.

Let's start with the most obvious one, because it's also one that people routinely screw up: know the rules.

Sounds simple, right?

Well, is your league full PPR, half-PPR or standard scoring? How many wide receivers start? How many flex spots are there? Is it a one-quarterback league or superflex? Are passing touchdowns worth four points or six? Do you get bonuses for long touchdowns or 100-yard games?

How many bench spots does everyone have? How does the waiver/free agency system work after the draft?

All of that matters.

A player can have significantly more value in one scoring system than another. A league that starts three wide receivers and a flex puts a lot more pressure on wide receiver depth than one that starts two receivers. Superflex leagues push quarterbacks way up the board.

So before you start obsessing over whether Player A should be ranked 37th or 41st, make sure you understand the game you're actually playing.

And that includes roster rules.

I've seen people get halfway through a draft before realizing the league adjusted the roster spots between seasons. I've seen people draft like they're playing standard scoring when receptions are worth a full point.

Don't be that person.

This is especially important if you're playing in multiple leagues. If the setup is different enough, an elite draft in one league might be a last-place roster in another.

Honestly, just knowing the rules probably puts you ahead of at least one player in your league (but likely more than one).

This is one of the most important parts of fantasy football drafting, and I don't think people talk about it nearly enough.

Who are you playing against?

There's a huge difference between a casual home league and a league filled with people who spend all summer studying fantasy football.

Maybe you're in a league with 11 friends you've known since college. Three of them are really into fantasy football. Five pay attention once the calendar flips to September but not one day sooner. One guy still thinks it's 2022.

Then there's Derek, who forgot the draft was today. Side note: definitely don't be this guy. There's nothing worse than those frantic phone calls to first locate "Derek" and then, if unsuccessful, calls to find a last-minute fill-in.

Home leagues are a completely different environment from a competitive league where nearly everyone understands Average Draft Position (ADP), knows the depth charts and has already done 50 drafts. If that's your league, I'm not sure why you're reading my fantasy football advice in the first place.

In a casual league, good players tend to fall further. There's often no reason to reach aggressively for someone just because you like him. There's a decent chance your league mates aren't even looking at the same players you are.

Sharper leagues are different. Sleepers aren't really sleepers when everyone knows about them. A player you think is going to last another round might have six other people waiting to draft him.

You also need to know the specific people in your league.

Home leagues develop personalities over time. One guy always takes a quarterback early. Another drafts rookies like he's waiting for his shot to be an actual NFL GM (it's not going to happen, Kevin). Someone else has to get at least three players from his favorite team every year.

Pay attention.

NFL COACHES AND EXECUTIVES SAY PATRICK MAHOMES IS NO LONGER THE BEST QUARTERBACK IN THE NFL

I live in Connecticut, and I've made this same point about NCAA Tournament pools. Filling out a bracket against a bunch of UConn fans is different because you already know UConn is probably going to be more popular in that pool than it would be nationally.

Fantasy football works the same way.

Drafting with a room full of Eagles fans? Philadelphia players probably aren't slipping very far.

And after 10 or 15 years in the same home league, you probably know your friends' bad habits better than they do. In fact, they probably don't even realize their own bad habits. Now is the time to use that information against them.

Are you drafting on ESPN? Yahoo? Sleeper? CBS? NFL?

Or are you sitting in someone's garage with a giant draft board and a stack of stickers?

Those are not the same drafts.

Every fantasy platform has its own rankings and its own ADP. And whether people realize it or not, those rankings sitting on the screen have a huge influence on who gets drafted when.

A player ranked near the top of the available list is going to attract attention.

Maybe you're using rankings from an analyst who has a certain wide receiver ranked 45th overall. Great. But your league is drafting on a site where that player typically goes around No. 70.

Why take him at 45?

You might be right about the player. But the entire point is to get him as late as you reasonably can.

That's why you need to check the site you're actually using. A player you have to grab in the sixth round on ESPN might still be sitting there in the eighth on Yahoo.

And that's before you even get to live drafts.

There isn't one universal list controlling the room when you're sitting around a table. One person has a printout from ESPN. Another has rankings from some fantasy analyst he follows. Someone is drafting off his phone.

Then there's the guy who bought a fantasy magazine in an airport six weeks ago (this guy usually falls into the "Mike Evans plays for who?!" category).

Good luck figuring out what he's going to do.

Those drafts can get weird quickly, which is part of what makes them fun.

This ties directly into the previous point.

Rankings are your opinion, or somebody else's opinion, of how players should be valued. ADP tells you where people are actually taking them.

You need to know both because that's how you're going to find value.

Let's say you absolutely love a player and have him ranked 50th overall. His ADP is around 80.

You have pick No. 52.

Taking him there isn't necessarily wrong if you believe he's worth the pick.

But what if you also select again at No. 69 (nice) and there's a very good chance he's still going to be available?

Now you've got a decision to make.

Fantasy football isn't just about identifying good players. It's also about figuring out how long you can afford to wait before somebody else takes them.

Of course, ADP isn't some magical law that everyone has to follow. Players get picked ahead of ADP all the time, and sometimes that's the right move.

Same thing with rankings.

There isn't nearly enough certainty in fantasy football to pretend that the player ranked 42nd is definitely better than the player ranked 49th. They're probably pretty close.

That's why tiers can be useful.

You might have six wide receivers that you view almost identically who are all still available. Meanwhile, there's one running back left before you see a significant drop at the position.

That matters a lot more than whether WR18 is technically ranked three spots ahead of RB17.

It happens in almost every fantasy draft.

Three quarterbacks go in quick succession.

Then someone takes another one.

Suddenly, a person who had absolutely no intention of drafting a quarterback starts thinking, "Oh no, I need to get one."

Do you?

Maybe. But it's also possible four people just helped you by taking quarterbacks while good players at other positions sat there.

Obviously, you can't completely ignore a run. If the last quarterback you really like is sitting there and six have already gone, you might have to pull the trigger.

But that's different from getting nervous because the room suddenly decided now is the time to grab QB1.

There are drafts where jumping into the run makes sense. There are others where I'm perfectly happy watching everyone else do it and taking whatever good players they're leaving for me.

This is called "board texture" if you're really into fantasy football, and I promise that's the last time I'm going to use a nerdy term like that.

There's something satisfying about looking at your fantasy team during the draft and seeing every starting position filled.

Quarterback? Got one.

Running backs? Done.

Wide receivers? Check.

Tight end? Taken care of.

Defense and kicker? Yep, got them, too.

Great.

Nobody gives you bonus points for that.

Your goal isn't to be the first person in the league with a complete Week 1 starting lineup. You're trying to build a roster for an entire season.

Maybe there's a tight end you like, but there are four others you'd be perfectly happy drafting later. Meanwhile, a running back you had ranked much higher than the rest of the board is still available even though you already have two running backs.

I'm probably taking RB3 and dealing with tight end later.

Obviously, this has limits. You can't completely ignore roster construction and just draft 14 running backs because they're the highest-ranked player every time you're on the clock.

But I see people pass on good players all the time because they don't like seeing an empty spot next to "TE" or "QB" on the draft screen.

Everyone loves sleepers.

It's one of the best parts of fantasy football, and if you Google "fantasy football sleepers" you'll probably get 10,000 results. Why? Every analyst writes those articles because they know how many people are looking for that exact analysis.

There's no better feeling than taking the guy no one in your league has even heard of and having him post a 1,000-yard, 10 TD season. Now you get to talk about what a football expert you are (but you're still not getting that GM gig, Kevin).

The problem is that fantasy players sometimes get so excited about finding sleepers that they destroy the entire point of finding them.

A player isn't much of a bargain if you draft him four rounds ahead of where anyone else was going to take him.

Now, there's nothing wrong with reaching sometimes. In fact, you have to do it.

Fantasy drafts don't let you select whenever you want. Maybe you pick 65th and don't pick again until 88th. There's a player with an ADP around 78 whom you really want.

Take him.

Waiting around for some perfect ADP value is a good way to watch the guy picking three spots behind you draft all the players you wanted.

But taking someone 15 picks early because you know he won't make it back to you is different from taking someone 50 picks early because you watched two preseason highlights and fell in love.

And, yes, maybe you really did find the next superstar.

I'd still rather draft him later if I can.

You can do 100 mock drafts before your real draft (but you shouldn't, because this is a major waste of time).

It won't matter.

Someone is going to take a player 25 picks earlier than expected. A player you've never seen fall past the fifth round is going to be sitting there in the seventh. You're going to have three players queued up for your next pick and watch all three come off the board right before you're on the clock.

Welcome to fantasy football.

This is why I never go into a draft thinking things like, "I'm definitely taking two running backs with my first two picks."

Maybe that's how it works out.

Then again, maybe the second round comes around and a receiver you never expected to see is sitting there.

Same with waiting for a quarterback, taking an elite tight end early or any other draft strategy you decided on before the first team was even on the clock.

Having a plan is smart. Just don't spend the entire draft trying to force the board to match the mock draft you did Tuesday night.

I saved this one for last because I think people sometimes forget it.

Fantasy football is supposed to be fun.

Yes, we all want to win. Winning is a lot more fun than losing. And everything written above is designed to help you make better decisions during your draft.

But you're also going to spend the next four months rooting for these players.

You'll watch a random Monday Night Football game between two teams you don't care about because you need 11 points from your wide receiver (I'm looking at you, Falcons at Saints in Week 4). You'll spend Sunday afternoon checking your phone to see whether your running back got credit for a reception (c'mon, that wasn't a lateral; he definitely threw it forward!)

You're going to care about these guys.

So, if there's a player you really like, and you want him on your fantasy team, take him.

Maybe it's your favorite player. Maybe you just really want to root for the guy this season. That's good enough for me. Take him.

Does that mean you should take someone with a 10th-round ADP in the third round because you really like him?

Probably not.

But we're talking about fantasy football here, not managing your 401(k) (unless you're in a league where you're playing for the value of someone's 401(k), but again, you're probably not taking advice from me if that's the case).

So pick a player a little earlier than ADP if you really want him. Who cares if some fantasy expert has another guy ranked two spots higher?

Do your homework. Understand the room you're drafting in and try not to light value on fire for no reason.

After that, get some players you actually like.

You might even win the league. If you do, don't forget to tell everyone how good you are at fantasy football.

And if you don't, blame injuries and bad luck.

That's what everyone else does.

item.title: Dad of third-grade girl in Massachusetts allegedly barged in on by trans student in bathroom calls for action
item.description: Massachusetts father of third grader alleges transgender student barged in girls stalls and is taking complaint to federal level.
item.content:encoded:
The Massachusetts father of a third-grade girl who says his daughter was subjected to a disturbing bathroom incident involving a transgender classmate is not backing down from his fight with the school district.

Luis Rivera, whose daughter attends Rochester Memorial School, has hired attorney Sam Whiting of the Massachusetts Liberty Legal Center after filing a federal Title IX complaint against the Old Rochester Regional School District in May.

A letter filed by Whiting on Rivera’s behalf alleges that Rivera’s 9-year-old daughter was the victim of sex-based harassment after a transgender female classmate, who was born male, entered her bathroom stall. The letter also alleges that the student had previously watched female students use the bathroom, which Rivera and his attorney argue invaded their privacy and undermined their dignity.

Rivera and his wife, Kerri, along with other parents, have repeatedly contacted Rochester Memorial School Principal Heidi Letendre about the transgender student’s use of the girls’ bathroom, according to the letter.

WASHINGTON MOTHER SAYS SHE FOUND ADULT MALE SHOWERING IN WOMEN'S LOCKER ROOM DURING CHILDREN'S SWIM MEET

"On numerous occasions, during this actual event, we reached out multiple times. And we were told by the principal that no boy is supposed to be in the bathroom. Then somewhere along the line, they changed their story," Rivera told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to Letendre for comment.

Rivera said he has attended every school committee meeting since the incident, joining other community members in pushing the district to change its bathroom policy.

He also said he and his wife have decided to remove their daughter from the school for the upcoming school year. His daughter wrote a letter to President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump asking for help with the situation.

"I feel scared to use the girls' bathroom," she wrote.

WASHINGTON MOTHER PULLS CHILDREN FROM SCHOOL AFTER PRIDE LESSON SHOWN IN MUSIC CLASS WITHOUT NOTICE

The dispute centers not only on the alleged incident involving Rivera’s daughter but also on the district’s interpretation of state and federal anti-discrimination laws, Whiting said.

Massachusetts law prohibits discrimination against students based on protected characteristics, including gender identity, and bars schools from excluding students from "the advantages, privileges and courses of study" they offer.

The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education also says transgender students should have access to school facilities, including bathrooms, consistent with their gender identity.

For now, however, the Old Rochester Regional School District does not appear to have plans to change its policy regarding transgender students.

In a message to parents, Superintendent Michael Nelson said that, following a Title IX investigation, school staff and district administrators acted in compliance with the law. The decision, he said, was made by an independent decision maker following the complaint brought forward by the Rochester Memorial School parent.

TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS WOKE SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF HIDING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

In a written statement, Nelson said the district is bound by the Massachusetts laws.

"Additionally, our schools adhere to the policies and procedures of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education," he said.

"... We believe that we are bound by law and state education policy and that age-appropriate handling of student matters in a public school setting is best left to the professional educators who know how to do their jobs correctly and effectively," he said.

He also noted that during this process, his educators and administrators have been subject to "innumerable explicit, angry and threatening communications," directly and indirectly through social media.

Fox News Digital reached out directly to Nelson.

Whiting said he and the parents involved are particularly disappointed by the superintendent’s response, which he claims downplayed the seriousness of the incident.

According to Whiting, the response amounted to, "Oh, these things just happen between 9-year-olds… sometimes bathroom doors are unlocked and these things happen."

PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT

Whiting said he hopes the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights will investigate the complaint.

"Ultimately, we hope they will find that the school district is in violation of Title IX and will refer the case to the Department of Justice for enforcement," he said. "School districts who violate Title IX can be at risk of losing their federal funds… We’re always hopeful they’ll do the right thing, but if they don’t, our plan is to try to get this in front of the proper authorities at the federal level."

Rivera said the lack of what he considers meaningful action from the district has left him with no choice but to escalate the matter.

"They haven’t taken any remedial action. And so that’s why we feel like we have to kind of bring this up to the higher authorities and the federal government," Rivera said. "There’s no transparency. There’s no accountability. It’s just they’re running around free, and they’re violating these girls’ privacy rights, because what happened to my daughter should have never happened if the policies were put into place."

"And I have to deal with her emotional trauma behind this," Rivera added.

EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

SECOND LADY USHA VANCE FIRES BACK AT POINTED JAB FROM DEMOCRATIC SENATE NOMINEE ABDUL EL-SAYED

TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES

In 2018, El-Sayed expressed support for allowing illegal immigrants to obtain standard driver's licenses, though he did not specifically push for those in the country illegally to receive the commercial driver's licenses necessary to operate long-haul trucks.

item.title: Trump's White House ballroom construction gets another lifeline from SCOTUS amid heated legal fight
item.description: Chief Justice John Roberts warned the White House ballroom project is "likely unlawful," but the Supreme Court let construction continue for now.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court has again sided with the Trump administration, allowing construction on the White House ballroom project to continue while the case continues to be litigated in the lower courts.

The court split 5-4 in granting the emergency request. The decision replaces a temporary order Chief Justice John Roberts issued just hours before a lower-court ruling blocking the work was set to take effect. The underlying litigation will continue in the lower courts, but court documents indicate key parts of the project could be completed within months, potentially outpacing the legal process.

Roberts issued a strongly worded dissent from the latest order, declaring that construction of the ballroom is "likely unlawful" and warning that allowing the project to proceed risks infringing on Congress’ constitutional powers.

"The President ordered the demolition of the East Wing of the White House to make way for a new, privately funded state ballroom in its place," Roberts wrote. "Construction of the ballroom has proceeded apace for the better part of a year."

TRUMP’S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM FOES FACE ‘VERY TOUGH ARGUMENT’ AT SUPREME COURT, LEGAL EXPERTS SAY

"That construction is likely unlawful," he wrote.

Roberts pointed to federal law that prohibits the construction of any "building or structure" on federal government parkland in Washington, D.C., without express authorization from Congress.

APPEALS COURT SAYS FEDERAL JUDGE MUST RECONSIDER BLOCKING WH BALLROOM, WEIGH NATIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS

The chief justice argued that the ballroom falls squarely within that restriction because it is being built on President’s Park, federal land that encompasses the White House and surrounding grounds.

"The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds—President’s Park—in the District of Columbia," Roberts wrote. "Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the Executive’s construction of it."

TRUMP SAYS WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM RULING JEOPARDIZES LIVES OF FUTURE PRESIDENTS, VOWS SUPREME COURT APPEAL

The Supreme Court’s decision allows construction to continue while the underlying legal challenge plays out, but it does not settle the ultimate question of whether the ballroom project is lawful.

The case remains in litigation in the lower courts, meaning Roberts’ assertion that the construction is "likely unlawful" represents his view in dissent rather than a final determination by the Supreme Court.

DOJ CITES WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING IN PUSH TO DROP LAWSUIT AGAINST BALLROOM

Roberts also took issue with the court’s treatment of Alison Hoagland, who originally challenged the project, arguing that both the historic nature of the White House and her interest in its preservation deserved greater weight.

"The White House is not just any building, and—when it comes to historic preservation—Hoagland is not just any person," Roberts wrote.

REPUBLICANS QUESTION TRUMP'S 'PRIVATELY FUNDED' BALLROOM AFTER REPORT POINTS TO TAXPAYER BURDEN

"In failing to appreciate as much, the Court misconceives the plaintiff’s injury, allowing the Executive’s likely infringement of the Legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue," he wrote.

"Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers."

Roberts closed his dissent by invoking former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and issuing a pointed warning about how decisions involving the White House are made.

"Winston Churchill once remarked that ‘[w]e shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us,’" Roberts wrote.

"All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House."

"I respectfully dissent," he wrote.

In addition to Roberts, Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson also dissented.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME

item.title: New report exposes intact Iranian bunker that may hide regime's ongoing nuclear work
item.description: The bunkered Natanz structure was built between 2010 and 2017, raising urgent questions about Iran's uranium enrichment capabilities after two wars.
item.content:encoded:
A new report from a leading think tank has revealed what it says is a partially submerged Iranian uranium facility at the Natanz nuclear compound in Iran.

The revelation of the secretive facility raises new concerns over whether Iran’s nuclear weapons apparatus was destroyed during the two American-Israeli-launched wars against the regime in 2025 and 2026.

The Washington, D.C.-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) announced in late August that it has located an underground Iranian facility that is likely linked to uranium enrichment for the possible use in production of atomic weapons.

EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE

It wrote that "The facility does not appear to have been targeted in the military actions of either 2025 or 2026. Since the June 2025 war, no vehicle activity has been observed at the facility in available satellite imagery."

According to the institute, "The Institute has identified a separately enclosed, partially below-ground, bunkered building at the Natanz Nuclear Complex that was likely intended to serve as uranium hexafluoride… storage facility to support large-scale uranium enrichment at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant. The bunkered structure was constructed between 2010 and 2017, with the bulk of construction occurring between 2015 and 2017."

It further added that "The lesson for today is that any temporary enrichment ban must include a dismantlement and dissolution of remaining capabilities and must not allow for any type of preparatory activity for the end of a ban."

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

Uranium is the crucial material to produce atomic weapons. Iran’s regime is vehemently opposed to the Trump administration’s demands that it stop enriching uranium and hand over its already enriched uranium.

According to another report by the Institute for Science and International Security in April," From December 2024 to June 2025, a half-year period, Iran almost doubled its stock of 60% enriched uranium to 440 kilograms. This action dramatically increased suspicion that Iran was moving toward a decision to build nuclear weapons, significantly shortening timelines to be able to create a nuclear arsenal with up to ten nuclear weapons."

The U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran’s vast nuclear weapons facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 significantly set back Iran’s ability to produce atomic weapons and enrich uranium.

OBAMA-ERA INSPECTION FLAWS IN IRAN COULD PERSIST AS EXPERTS WARN OF NUCLEAR BLIND SPOTS

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "The report assesses the structure at the Natanz nuclear facility was not targeted during Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury. This raises questions as to why the U.S. and Israel did not target the site. Given that Iran is not allowing IAEA [International Atomic Energy Agency] inspections of bombed facilities, in contravention of its NPT [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons]obligations, this will require Washington and Jerusalem to rely on their own intelligence estimates as to this bunkered building."

Brodsky added, "If it is still intact and can accommodate this kind of enrichment activity, the site should be destroyed in any future strikes. The allowance of such a facility under the JCPOA [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action] demonstrates the flaws of the agreement — permitting Iran to retain an industrial scale enrichment program following the sunsets of various provisions — and underscores why zero enrichment in Iran has to continue to be the international demand."

When asked about the facility and if the IAEA plans to inspect it, Fredrik Dahl, a spokesman for the IAEA, told Fox News Digital, that "The building you are referring to is well-known to the Agency as part of the Natanz site that the IAEA regularly inspected prior to mid-2025."

Asked about the report, Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, told Fox News Digital that "First, Iran’s nuclear facilities were totally obliterated during Operation Midnight Hammer. Now, Operation Economic Outcast is severing every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran. President Trump has been clear that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon, and America is entering the endgame with the single greatest financial offensive ever mounted against an adversary."

Successive U.S. administrations have repeatedly designated the Islamic Republic of Iran since the 1980s as a leading state-sponsor of terrorism.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement last week that the U.S. imposed the economic equivalent of the military campaign that defeated Nazi Germany on the Islamic Republic of Iran could set off a series of events leading to the dissolution of the nearly 47-year-old dictatorship in Tehran, according to experts.

Bessent’s declaration of economic warfare — formally designated Operation Economic Outcast — follows President Trump’s commitment to launch an "economic D-Day" against the clerical regime. The comprehensive U.S. economic pressure point campaign also aims to isolate the regime with respect to its efforts to rebuild its nuclear weapons facility.

item.title: Texas learns the hard way not to mock Florida high school football, Lindsey Vonn stuns & USC's poor showing!
item.description: A Texas high school football team learned a brutal lesson after disrespecting Florida's St. Thomas Aquinas, trailing 38-0 by halftime Friday night.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Final day of August, folks. This is it. At 12:01, we officially begin the 'Ber months — otherwise known as the greatest stretch on the sports calendar.

Forget sports ... it's the greatest stretch on the calendar, period.

September. October. November. December. Four of the best months of the year, staring us right in our fat faces. How lucky are we?

We got our college football appetizer on Saturday, and it starts in full this week. We get NFL next Wednesday (!!!). We have a three-day weekend coming up. Fantasy football drafts are in full swing. The WNBA is taking the next three weeks off.

Again, who has it better than us? Labor Day, Halloween, Thanksgiving, Christmas. Unreal stretch coming up. Strap in and hold on tight. We're in for a wild little ride.

Welcome to a Monday Nightcaps — the one where a Texas high school football team learns the hard way not to disrespect the great state of Florida. This was never, ever going to end well.

What else? I've got Lindsey Vonn smashing tennis balls and dominating in a green dress, my Red Sox got embarrassed over the weekend, and let's talk about that USC crowd from Saturday afternoon. It was pathetic, and for those screaming about it being a blowout Week 0 game, I've got some highlights out of South Dakota to show you.

Give me a break.

Grab you something tall and strong — but please don't make it a hurricane (we're entering PEAK time down here) — and settle in for a final-Monday-of-August 'Cap!

Obviously, the end of August and beginning of the 'Ber months hit just a bit different down here in Florida.

Case in point: We're currently spending the week monitoring 'Dolly,' which is, unfortunately, the next named storm on the list. Looks like we're just gonna get some possible rain remnants from her later this week, which is fine. Not the best, given it's rained all summer where I am, but better than the alternative.

But it is a reminder that this is the time of year where the H-words really get active. This is a 'hold-your-breath' month for Floridians. Let's keep our heads down and eyes on the prize, folks. Let's GRIND.

OK, let's get this class going by staying this great state and checking out last Friday's big national game between DeSoto (Texas) and St. Thomas Aquinas down in Fort Lauderdale:

Hilarious. St. Thomas, by the way, has won seven straight state championships. They've been a Florida powerhouse since I was in school, and that was a long time ago.

USC FOOTBALL RIPPED FOR PATHETIC CROWD AT HOME OPENER: 'ABSOLUTELY EMBARRASSING'

There's always been this debate surrounding high school football ... which state produces the best talent? It's either Florida, Georgia, Texas or California. Those are the Big Four. I'd throw in Tennessee as well.

Obviously, I'm biased. Duh. I live and breathe Florida. We have the greatest governor in the world, had no clue COVID was happening, and have so much leftover money in the budget we're about to nix property taxes (kinda). I played high school football down here. I covered it for years.

I don't think it's particularly close.

Don't poke the bear like that, DeSoto! Dumb decision. They went down, 38-0, in the first half and the second half took 15 minutes because there was a running clock.

It Just Means More down here!

You know where it doesn't mean more ... or, frankly, anything?

Southern California:

Goodness gracious. I know it was San Jose State, but come on. That's just pathetic.

It was so bad, by the way, that USC felt the need to issue a STATEMENT on the attendance:

"We understand the factors that impacted Saturday’s attendance," USC said, via USA Today. "We have high expectations and a premier home schedule this season, and we know the competitive advantage an electric Coliseum atmosphere can provide our program. We thank our fans who showed up Saturday and look forward to seeing increased attendance the rest of the season."

Factors? What factors? The heat? It was 92 degrees. Give me a break.

And no, I don't want to hear the "it was San Jose State!" argument. That's so weak. Guess who South Dakota State played on Saturday?

The Stetson Hatters — otherwise known as, quite possibly, the worst team in all of college football. I know this, because I spent many years in DeLand. The Jackrabbits, a nationally ranked FCS team, were a 49.5 point favorite. I know this, because I hammered that and it was the easiest win I've ever had.

They won 70-7.

LOOK at this crowd for that game Saturday night:

Spare me, USC. Don't bulls–t a bullsh–tter.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Monday class into a big Monday night. First up? My Red Sox got embarrassed in New York this weekend, losing a winnable series, 3-1, because they chose to basically punt in two of the games. It was a disgrace, and the bellyaching from Red Sox Twitter today has been even worse.

Everyone is complaining about this 'no catch' call from yesterday afternoon, which basically turned a 0-0 game on its head:

I thought it was a catch in real time, and thought it was a catch after the replay. But, it was ruled a no-catch on the field, and they were never overturning that — especially at Yankee Stadium.

But the whining and complaining afterwards was a sight to behold, and I'm a Red Sox fan!

It got so bad, the Red Sox radio team started telling our crappy pitchers to start hitting their crappy players.

Seriously:

Good God. It's so pathetic. I like Will Middlebrooks. I don't particularly love Will Flemming. This was just insane to hear.

Hey, fellas — it's Red Sox/Yankees. This was the biggest game of the year. Quit whining about the stupid catch, quit whining about Jazz stealing third, and maybe start talking about how the Red Sox were a complete no-show all weekend long.

You're either the hunter or the hunted, and the Red Sox laid three eggs in the biggest series of the year and then whined about it for five innings yesterday.

Grow up and start worrying more about not sucking in Yankee Stadium. You're gonna be back there in a month.

Figure it out.

Whew. OK, I needed to get that off my chest. Appreciate everyone allowing me to do so.

Let's cool down with Lindsey Vonn on the way out.

And, of course, let's have a big week.

Was it a catch? Email me at Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

item.title: Stephen A Smith reveals Barack Obama privately called him after Biden criticism ahead of 2024 election
item.description: Stephen A. Smith revealed Barack Obama called him before the 2024 election to discuss his impact, but would not appear on his podcast publicly.
item.content:encoded:
Podcast host Stephen A. Smith revealed on Friday that former President Barack Obama called him before the 2024 election to discuss his influence, noting that Obama wanted to speak privately rather than appear on his podcast.

"What I never told y'all, and I never brought up, is that Barack Obama called me too. The content of that conversation will remain private because I will not violate trust," Smith said. "He called before the election to discuss my impact, but he didn't come on the podcast either."

Smith spoke to "The Culture Table," hosted by Tori Cooper, Sumatra Abernathy and Ashley Christopher, about receiving a "thumbs-down" award from the National Association of Black Journalists (NABJ) at an Atlanta gala, defending himself against the criticism.

STEPHEN A SMITH CALLS OUT JILL BIDEN, DEMS FOR 'LYING THROUGH THEIR TEETH' AND DAMAGING PARTY'S BRAND

"It was after I said that we need a new president because Joe Biden clearly was done. You know, he clearly looked done. So the point is, folks like to talk to me privately, but then when I ask them to come on camera and to have a fruitful discussion, now they go elsewhere," he continued.

"So it's like I'm taking these hits, and these are people that want to facilitate or assist in the facilitation of these narratives being disseminated and projected about me. But the same people calling me privately, having discussions upon which I have never violated. This is the first time anyone has ever heard me publicly state that Barack Obama called me," Smith said.

OBAMA BLAMES SPLINTERED MEDIA FOR PREVENTING SUPERSTAR DEMOCRAT FROM RISING UP

The former president's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Obama wasn't the only one Smith accused of not coming on his show. He also named former first lady Michelle Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

"I think the Democrats fear my footsteps," he said. "I think they know that they have a legitimate fear that I can influence the election potentially. I will never divulge what was said, but last week when I did my podcast and I responded to the NABJ, I pointed out how Kamala Harris reached out to me and asked to meet with me, and we met for two hours."

KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN

"She did not speak to me and come on my show before the election," Smith said of Harris. "Once again, in my opinion, they take paths of smaller resistance."

Harris' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

AMERICA OWES BLACK WOMEN 'EVERYTHING,' REP JASMINE CROCKETT RANTS OVER JULY 4 WEEKEND

Smith recently addressed the NABJ's thumbs-down award during his show.

"The reality is that it was a personal hit job," Smith said. "We can sit up there and lollygag around and act like we don't know any better. It was a personal hit job. Which, by the way, usually doesn't phase me. I know you think something phases me, just because you see me commenting on it. No, I'm in this business. I have a platform. I can comment about anything I want to, and I will continue to do so."

"That's not what this is," he added. "This is different. This is a journalism organization that didn't engage in journalism when it came to critiquing me. Disparaging Black women is a very incendiary thing to say. If you felt that adamant about it, [NABJ] President [Errin] Haines, how come I never got a call?"

Smith speculated that the award was focused on his past criticism of high-profile Black female political figures like Crockett. He also revealed that he reached out to Haines regarding the organization's allegations to potentially discuss their differences, a conversation that ultimately went nowhere.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"While much of the public conversation in recent days has centered on Stephen A. Smith, he was one of five recipients named this year," the NABJ previously told Fox News Digital in a statement. "The concerns NABJ raised extend well beyond any one individual and include threats to editorial independence, the loss of newsroom diversity and reporting expertise, the treatment of Black journalists in the workplace, responsible use of influential media platforms, and decisions that affect the ability of journalists to fully and fairly cover Black communities and hold powerful institutions accountable."

"Bill Maher has shared the same sentiment: High-profile Democrats want nothing to do with his program, much as they avoid Stephen A. Smith's. item.title: DSA leader's working-class image takes hit as public records pile up contradictions
item.description: Gustavo Gordillo, NYC Democratic Socialists of America co-chair, faces scrutiny over claims about his immigrant parents, union status and housing.
item.content:encoded:
The contradictions are piling up around New York City Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Gustavo Gordillo, whose claims about his working-class credentials — from being a "union electrician" to his housing and family story — have increasingly collided with public records and other evidence.

Gordillo has repeatedly invoked his family’s immigrant success story while explaining his support for socialism.

"My parents came here, they had nothing," Gordillo told the New York Times in a profile piece earlier this month. "Their first jobs were in fast food and cleaning houses. They built success in this country. And they’re absolutely the exception."

According to Gordillo, he advances the cause of socialism because he believes it can "build a world" where his parents’ success story is "not exceptional."

LUXURY TRAVEL, SHOPPING, SIX-FIGURE INCOME: BATTLEGROUND DEMS RIPPED FOR 'PHONY' WORKING-CLASS NARRATIVE

A 2021 obituary for Gordillo’s paternal grandfather, however, raises questions about the family history behind that account, the New York Post reported Saturday. 

Manuel Gordillo, Gordillo’s grandfather, emigrated from Peru to the United States to practice medicine in 1958. After settling in the United States, Manuel met his future wife in St. Louis, and the couple later had Gordillo’s father, Gustavo, per the obituary.

The obituary also notes that Gordillo’s grandfather built a successful life as a psychiatrist in Ohio, at one point serving as the president of the Ohio Psychiatric Association, casting doubt on the socialist’s claim that his parents grew up in poverty.

"My dad, his first job in the United States was working at Wendy’s, my mom’s first job was a house cleaner, and they did make a living for themselves, and they had success," Gordillo told Fox News in July.

The elder Gordillo's obituary portrays him as a loving and active father, noting that he raised his "children in Lakewood, Ohio" and that "his most cherished role was as a husband, father, grandfather, and uncle/tio." 

"Gustavo and his parents were born in Peru and immigrated to the US," a New York City Democratic Socialists of America spokesperson told Fox News Digital following publication. "Gustavo’s father grew up in Peru, not in the United States, and the family had limited contact with Gustavo’s grandfather, who is the subject of the Post’s recent reporting."

Fox News Digital reached the New York City Democratic Socialists of America with follow-up questions on Monday evening. 

The questions surrounding Gordillo’s account of his family history come after discrepancies emerged over how he has described his occupation and living arrangements.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST HEADED FOR $142K LEGISLATURE SALARY BEGS FOR RENT HANDOUT, DELETES POST AFTER BACKLASH

The 38-year-old socialist, for example, told the New York Times that he was renting a modest apartment in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn only for it to be revealed that he was actually living in a $1.4 million townhouse owned by his father in a trendier part of the borough.

"Not only did DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo's parents buy him this rowhouse, they converted it from a two family and renovated it into a luxury single-family home for him," New York City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino said on X. "Exactly the kind of 'greed' the DSA rails against on a daily basis, and reducing valuable housing inventory by one more unit, which is supposedly something the DSA cares very deeply about."

FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY

Also undercutting Gordillo’s working-class image is his continued self-identification as a "union electrician" despite the fact that he hasn’t been a member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers since March, when he was fired for not showing up to his apprenticeship.

"After learning of Mr. Gordillo’s prolonged absence from and failure to participate in required work and classes, the trustees of the Joint Apprentice Training Committee terminated Mr. Gordillo from the program," the IBEW said in a statement.

Even with the IBEW publicly stating that Gordillo is not a member of their organization, the socialist leader still identifies himself as a "union electrician" on social media.

item.title: Popular artificial sweetener linked to potentially dangerous heart risk
item.description: A new study of over 17,700 participants links higher xylitol blood levels to increased cardiovascular risk, including heart attack and stroke, over future decades.
item.content:encoded:
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests.

The research, which was presented at the ESC Cardiology Congress in Germany this week, showed that higher levels of xylitol in the blood were associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute, according to the National Institutes of Health. It is often used in higher amounts to sweeten foods, drinks, chewing gum and dental care products.

ZERO-CALORIE SWEETENERS COULD ALTER THE GENES OF LATER GENERATIONS, NEW STUDY WARNS

The researchers followed two large study cohorts of more than 17,700 Canadian and British participants.

Over a six-year follow-up, people in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels.

Over 30 years, participants in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk group with the highest xylitol levels had an 18% greater risk of MACE.

Both cohorts showed evidence of a dose-dependent association, in which higher blood xylitol concentrations corresponded to higher rates of cardiovascular events.

DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'

These higher risks persisted even after the researchers adjusted for other factors like age, gender, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes and lipid levels.

The study follows previous research that showed xylitol can enhance the ability of platelets to form clots, according to Dr. Marco Witkowski, the study presenter from Charité University Hospital in Berlin, Germany.

"Artificial sweeteners are consumed by people who think they are healthier than sugar, and they are generally regarded as safe by regulatory agencies," the doctor said in a statement.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our long-term findings in the general population highlight how little we know about the cardiovascular safety of xylitol and indicate that further studies are warranted, especially as the amount of xylitol in products continues to increase."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study was observational and does not prove that xylitol causes cardiovascular events, as the researchers noted that more studies are needed to confirm the findings.

The report also does not establish whether high levels of xylitol in the blood necessarily reflect dietary consumption, as the sugar alcohol can also be produced naturally in the body as part of glucose metabolism.

"These disturbing findings with [a] plausible mechanism of xylitol increasing cardiovascular risk should be taken very seriously," Dr. Aseem Malhotra, a cardiologist and public health campaigner based in London, told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"As a practicing cardiologist, I see many patients suffering from anxiety and palpitations that resolve as soon as they stop taking artificial sweeteners."

Malhotra, who was not involved in the study, noted that one of the most important dietary changes to reduce cardiovascular risk is to "unsweeten your sweet tooth."

"That’s why I advise all my patients to avoid all processed sugars and artificial sweeteners for six weeks to break the addiction," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to several food and beverage trade groups for comment.

The district video later featured messages from Oregon Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley and Rep. Maxine Dexter, D-Ore., along with other Portland-area public figures.

Trump has made energy dominance and U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence central pillars of his second term, placing data centers at the center of his push to maintain America's edge over China.

"China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement," Trump wrote, arguing that resistance to new facilities risks undercutting America's edge in the global AI race.

The data center boom has also emerged as a midterm flashpoint, as concerns over rising electricity costs, water use and rapid development collide with promises of jobs, investment and U.S. dominance in artificial intelligence.

That tension is already playing out across the country.

Trump has specifically criticized Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's approach, calling the Lone Star State's stance toward data centers a "mistake" and pointing to the economic investment the projects can bring to communities willing to host them.

Texas has cemented its status as a heavyweight in the industry, with Dallas ranking as the world's No. 1 primary data center market in Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 Global Data Center Market Comparison. But billions of dollars in new investment have also brought enormous electricity demands and questions over who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support the boom.

Abbott has moved to address those concerns, directing regulators to ensure data centers cover the infrastructure costs needed to serve them and calling on developers to add their own power generation rather than shift costs onto Texas residents.

Meanwhile, in Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro recently imposed new requirements on large data center developments.

Other governors have taken a more restrictive stance. Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyper-scale data centers as states grapple with concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and the pace of development.

Data centers house the servers and computing equipment that power artificial intelligence and cloud services, requiring vast amounts of electricity to operate and cool. Most Americans may never see the inside of one, but they rely on data centers constantly, often without realizing it.

The growing patchwork of state restrictions and requirements could complicate Trump’s push for rapid data center expansion as communities weigh America’s AI ambitions against concerns over electricity costs, water use and development.
